fields.meaning: feeling uneasy or embarrassed in a situation
fields.nativePronunciation: /ˈɑːkwɚd/; /ˈɔːkwɚd/ is also used by American speakers. Stress the first syllable. The second syllable has an American r-colored vowel; do not use the vowel in cat.
fields.spanishPronunciation: La primera vocal no es /æ/ como en cat. En la segunda sílaba, mantén la r americana sin vibrarla como una r española. La aproximación escrita no sustituye al IPA ni al audio.
examples: She felt awkward staying silent during the meeting.
It was an awkward moment when the power went out.
He gave an awkward laugh after the joke fell flat.
They had an awkward conversation about money.
fields.usageNote: Use feel awkward to describe feeling uncomfortable in a situation. Awkward can also describe something difficult to use or handle; it is not limited to people or social situations.

fields.meaning: causing you to feel very tired or mentally exhausted
fields.category: Adjective, from the regular verb drain
fields.nativePronunciation: /ˈdreɪ.nɪŋ/ – stress on the first syllable; the “a” sounds like the “a” in “day”, and the final “‑ing” is pronounced with a short /ɪŋ/.
fields.spanishPronunciation: Empieza con /dr/ y el diptongo /eɪ/. En -ing, /ɪ/ no es la i española: cambia la posición de la lengua, no solo la duración. Termina con /ŋ/, sin añadir una g separada.
examples: The long commute was really draining after work.
Studying for finals can be draining if you don’t take breaks.
She found the constant noise in the office draining.
Running a marathon without proper training is draining.
fields.usageNote: Learners often mix up “draining” (describing the thing that causes fatigue) with “drained” (describing how a person feels). Use “draining” for the source of exhaustion.
alternatives: taking a lot out of me

edits.after: Adjective, from the regular verb drain

fields.meaning: past tense of go; traveled or moved to a place
fields.nativePronunciation: /wɛnt/. The vowel is like the one in bet. Keep the final /nt/ together without adding a vowel; the final t may be unreleased in natural speech.
fields.spanishPronunciation: Empieza con /w/, sin añadir una g. La vocal /ɛ/ es más abierta que la e española. Conserva /nt/ al final y no añadas una e después de la t.
examples: She went to the gym after work.
We went out for dinner last Friday.
They went to the office early to finish the paperwork.
He went back home to get his laptop.
fields.usageNote: Common mistake: using “go” instead of the past form “went” when talking about a completed action. Remember “went” is only for past events.

fields.frontExample: Let's not put off this conversation.
fields.nativePronunciation: /pʊt ˈɔf/; off also has /ɑf/ in American speech. Link the final t into the next vowel. Phrase stress can change with emphasis; do not assume put is always stressed.
fields.spanishPronunciation: Empieza put con /p/, no con /s/. La vocal /ʊ/ no es exactamente la u española. En off, mantén /f/ al final sin añadir una vocal.
examples: We put off the meeting until next week.
She keeps putting off her dentist appointment.
I’ve put it off long enough.
Don’t put off talking to your manager.
fields.usageNote: With a pronoun, put it between the two parts: put it off, not put off it. A noun can follow off or go between the parts: put off the meeting / put the meeting off.

fields.meaning: to make something stronger or more intense, especially a disagreement or debate
fields.nativePronunciation: /ˈfjuːəl/. Start with /fj/ and move from /uː/ toward the weak vowel /ə/ before l. Some speakers compress the syllables; do not describe the stressed vowel as /ʊ/ in book.
fields.spanishPronunciation: Empieza con /f/ seguida de un deslizamiento /j/, como la y inicial inglesa de yes. Pasa de /uː/ hacia una vocal débil antes de la l; una aproximación española no reproduce todos los sonidos.
examples: The new evidence fueled the debate.
His angry speech fueled the crowd’s frustration.
Social media can fuel rumors.
The team’s recent win has fueled hopes for a championship.
fields.usageNote: In this context, fuel is a verb: something fuels an argument, fear, or speculation by making it stronger. The regular American past spelling is fueled. The noun fuel also means a substance used for energy.
fields.spanishTranslation: alimentar / avivar (una discusión o un sentimiento)
